entries.text: Last paper done. When the invigilator said pens down the hall went so quiet. 終於完咗。

Last DSE paper today. Everyone went to celebrate in Mong Kok and I went along, but I felt strangely empty. For six years the plan was just “get through the exam”. Now there's no plan. What am I supposed to want next?

content.title: The exams ended, and so did the plan
content.headline: The exams ended, and so did the plan
content.body:
Hey Kit,

Six years of DSE, and this afternoon the hall went quiet when the last paper ended. Then you went out to Mong Kok with everyone and felt strangely empty in the middle of the celebration.

That emptiness makes sense. For six years the plan was simply to get through, and today the plan finished before the next one existed. What you're feeling isn't failure. It's the space a very big goal leaves behind when it's gone. You asked what you're supposed to want next, and the honest answer is that you don't have to know this week.

The clues usually turn up when nothing is scheduled. So for once, let the days be a bit empty on purpose.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.headline: A hike that didn't need to be useful
content.body:
Hey Kit,

You climbed Dragon's Back with your cousin and, for a whole afternoon, nobody mentioned results or the future. Just snacks, the view, and a head that finally felt quiet.

Notice where that quiet came from. It wasn't from having answers. It came from being outside, with someone easy, doing something that didn't have to be useful. After weeks of thinking about what comes next, your mind rested the moment it had something real in front of it.

That's a good thing to remember on the louder days ahead.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.title: Results day: good enough, but not a reason
content.headline: Results day: good enough, but not a reason
content.body:
Hey Kit,

You refreshed the results page about twenty times this morning, and your mum called before you'd even opened it. By tonight the scores were good enough for business, the choices were reordered around what fits, and you felt nothing much at all.

Feeling flat about a major isn't a sign you've chosen wrong. Most of this decision was made by numbers and by what feels safe to your family, so of course it doesn't feel like yours yet. A choice can become yours later, through the parts of it you end up caring about.

You don't need to love it today. You only need to keep an eye out for the bits that make you curious.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.title: Four friends, four different places

content.body:
Hey Kit,

Manchester, Taiwan, another uni across town, and you. Four friends, four places, and everyone else sounded excited while you felt like you were just going where your results took you.

It's easy to compare your quiet start with their loud announcements. But they're describing a plan, not how it will actually feel in October. Nobody knows that yet, them included. What's true tonight is that the four of you are changing at the same time, and that's worth marking together rather than measuring.

A last dinner won't fix the distance, but it gives the change a proper goodbye.

content.title: The offer came: relief, and a question mark
content.headline: The offer came: relief, and a question mark
content.body:
Good morning, Kit.

The BBA offer arrived, your mum cried a little from relief, and you were relieved too. Then someone asked what you want to do with business, and there was nothing to say.

Let's separate two things. The offer answers where you'll study. It doesn't answer what you'll do, and it was never meant to. People who ask that question usually just want a sentence, not a life plan. A simple, honest line you can say without pressure will take a lot of weight out of those conversations.

The bigger answer will come from what you notice over the next year. Keep track of it.

All the best,
Your mentor

You saw Hei off at the airport tonight, and on the bus home it hit you: you'll start uni without knowing a single person there. Then you kept scrolling back through old photos.

Both things are true at once. You're losing the easy closeness of having your people nearby, and you're about to walk into rooms full of strangers. Missing them this much isn't weakness. It's what it looks like when a friendship has been good.

A message for when Hei's plane lands keeps the thread warm, and starting from zero at uni is something you only have to do one person at a time.

Hey Kit,

Hundreds of people, cheering and games all day, and you smiled and followed along. At lunch everyone was already in groups of five, so you ate a siu mai standing up. You came home tired from pretending to be fine.

Big loud crowds are a hard place to meet anyone, especially when you're quieter. Talking to two people today wasn't a failure; it was what a crowd like that allows. You'll probably find your people somewhere smaller, where there's something to do besides shout.

So this week, skip the biggest events and look for one small group built around an activity.

Talk soon,
Your friend

Hey Kit,

Three weeks in, and lunch alone again, pretending to be busy on your phone. The old group chat is getting quieter, and you're wondering whether you're even in the right place. You also wrote, in Cantonese, that you really want to make friends but don't know how to start.

That last line matters most. You're not lonely because there's something wrong with you. In secondary school, friendship came with the timetable; here you have to choose a door and walk through it, and nobody tells you which one. That's new for almost everyone, even the people who look settled.

Starting from what you're curious about makes the first step much less scary.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.title: Is business really yours?
content.headline: Is business really yours?
content.body:
Good morning, Kit.

Accounting midterm next week, an afternoon of group study that turned into everyone comparing Big 4 applications, and a question you couldn't shake: is this what you want, or what you're supposed to want?

That's a good question to ask, and you don't need to answer it under exam pressure. Here's a way to look at it. Over the past month, your best moments have been a photo walk, a seat saved on a minibus, a slide your tutor liked. None of them were about internships. That doesn't mean business is wrong; it means your evidence about yourself is coming from somewhere else right now.

Collect that evidence for a while before you decide anything.

All the best,
Your mentor

content.title: The last tutoring session of term
content.headline: The last tutoring session of term
content.body:
Hey Kit,

The last tutoring session of term, and the kids made you a card thanking you for teaching them fractions. Jason drew you holding a camera. You're keeping it on your desk.

Think about what that drawing means. A kid who once wouldn't try fractions remembered both of your worlds: the tutor and the photographer. In one term you went from eating lunch alone to being someone a nine-year-old draws. That happened one Tuesday at a time.

Keep the card somewhere you'll see it on the harder days.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.title: You don't need the whole map yet
content.headline: You don't need the whole map yet
content.body:
Hi Kit,

It's you, a few years from now. Tonight you came home from the last photo walk of term, egg tarts and all, and wrote that three months ago you ate lunch alone and wondered if you were in the wrong place. Now you have Wing, the Saturday walks and the kids on Tuesdays.

You also wrote that you still don't know what job you want, but you know you like helping people figure things out. I want you to hear how much that is. It's a direction you found by living, not by planning: the guy at the door, Jason and his fractions, the questions you took to Dr Lam.

You don't need the whole map yet. Keep following that one thread.

With love,
You, later
